name: The World of AI: Power and Cooling datacenter electricity section
title: The World of AI: Power and Cooling datacenter electricity section
answer: The World of AI's Power and Cooling section is a short, daily re-verified page with three curated entries on how AI datacenters get electricity and cooling. Its most useful point is a cited Department of Energy 2024 LBNL finding: US datacenters used about 4.4% of electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, driven mainly by AI. The page frames this as a hard constraint on AI scaling, because grid expansion lags compute demand.

sections.body: The World of AI publishes this Power and Cooling section. It is a curated index page with three entries, each described as curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re-verified daily. It covers how AI datacenters get electricity and dispose of heat, including grid connection and interconnection queues, contracted generation, and the shift from air to liquid cooling. It points to separate sections for individual facilities and internal hardware. The page gives a retrieved date of 2026-09-28 and cites a Department of Energy 2024 LBNL report.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page states that its Power and Cooling section has three entries, each curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re-verified daily. It says the section covers how an AI datacenter gets electricity and gets rid of heat: grid connection and interconnection queues, the generation contracted to serve the load, and the shift from air to liquid cooling that dense GPU racks forced. It directs readers to separate sections for individual facilities and for racks and interconnect inside them. The main cited finding is from DOE's 2024 LBNL report: datacenters consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver. The page says this trajectory reflects a hard constraint on AI scaling, because the grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows. It argues that even modest adoption of AI training and inference at scale will require either new generation capacity, storage, or load shifting, none of which are built yet. It notes that the 6.7 to 12% range signals uncertainty about how fast AI deployment actually happens, depending on factors the electricity numbers alone cannot capture. The page also describes site-wide search across its database, including state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, glossary, tools directory, AI companies, research library, MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators, and weekly digests.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source attributes to DOE's 2024 LBNL report the figures of about 4.4% of US electricity consumed by datacenters in 2023 and a projected 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI as the driver. It states the section has three power and cooling entries, each curated with a verified vendor or primary source and re-verified daily. It positions the projection range as a sign of uncertainty and says the grid cannot expand as fast as compute demand grows. It says new generation capacity, storage, or load shifting are not built yet.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader tracking AI in Energy can use this page as a short pointer to a quantified power constraint. It gives a citable DOE-based trajectory for US datacenter electricity use and frames the bottleneck as grid expansion, generation, storage, and load shifting. It also names the operational topics that matter for AI datacenters, grid connection and interconnection queues, contracted generation, and the move from air to liquid cooling. Because the page is re-verified daily and gives a citation, it can serve as a current entry point, but the reader must follow the cited DOE report for the underlying analysis.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Energy

sections.body: The source is a section landing page, not the DOE report itself. It lists only three entries and does not reproduce their contents, so it gives no facility-level data, regional breakdown, methodology, or full definitions. It is partly commercial, as the page advertises books by Stephen R. Jordan, a novel, and a set of consulting audits. It is dated by a retrieved date of 2026-09-28 and cites a 2024 DOE LBNL report, so the projection may be overtaken. It does not cover other energy topics beyond the brief claims above.
